---
title: "Definition of the state of health"
---

*Status: **provisional** — version 0.1, 18 October 2026. This definition
is expected to change as the project learns what is measurable and what
matters. Each revision records its trigger and its changes. See
[Revision process](#revision-process).*

## Why provisional?

The project treats the state of health as dynamic and nonstationary
([Health is not stationary](nonstationarity.qmd)): the thing being
defined changes over time, and so does our understanding of it. Fixing a
definition permanently would contradict that premise. Instead the
definition is **versioned** — a working commitment that is good enough to
decide what to measure now, and explicit enough that revisions are visible
rather than silent.

The expectation is that the data landscape (milestone M2 in the
[roadmap](../ROADMAP.md)) will force revisions: some domains will prove
measurable, others will not; some proxies will turn out to track the
construct poorly.

## The definition (v0.1)

::: {.callout-note}
**The state of health of a population** is the joint condition of its
members across the domains of **mortality, physical morbidity, mental
health, functional status, subjective wellbeing, and social wellbeing**,
at a given time and place — including how that condition is distributed
within the population and how it is changing over time.
:::

Three features of the wording carry weight:

- **Joint condition.** The domains are not interchangeable and are not
  summed into a single number by definition. Any single number is an
  *index* built on top of the definition, not the definition itself.
- **Distribution.** The state of health is a distribution, not an average
  — inequalities are part of the state of health, not an add-on.
- **Changing.** The state of health is a trajectory, not a snapshot.
  From a decision perspective, we care about the **cumulative**
  (time-integrated) state of health over time — so actions are evaluated by
  their effect on cumulative outcomes, not only immediate levels.

## Conceptual basis

The definition builds on three established positions:

- **WHO's breadth.** Health is "a state of complete physical, mental and
  social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity"
  [@who1948]. This is why the definition has six domains rather than one,
  and why clinical status alone is insufficient.
- **The ICF's measurability.** The International Classification of
  Functioning, Disability and Health treats functioning and disability as
  outcomes of the interaction between health conditions and contextual
  factors, spanning body functions and structures, activities, and
  participation [@who2001icf]. This is what makes functional status a
  domain in its own right rather than a by-product of disease.
- **The capability approach's evaluative anchor.** Health matters because
  of what it enables people to do and be [@sen1999] — which is why
  subjective and social wellbeing are in scope, not just biology.

## Domains

| Domain | What it covers | Details |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Mortality | Premature and overall death, cause-of-death burden | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| Physical morbidity | Disease incidence and prevalence, chronic conditions, injury | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| Mental health | Mental health status and substance-use harms | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| Functional status | Functioning, disability, activities of daily living | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| Subjective wellbeing | Self-rated health, life satisfaction, positive wellbeing | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| Social wellbeing | Social connection, support, and participation | [Measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |

**Candidate additions.** Oral health, sensory health (vision and
hearing), and injury are currently folded into physical morbidity and
functional status. They may be promoted to domains if the data landscape
shows they can be measured distinctly and add information the current
domains miss. The bar for adding a domain is that it must not merely
duplicate an existing one.

**Cross-cutting dimensions.** Age and life-course stage, sex and gender,
Indigenous identity, and geography apply to every domain rather than
being domains themselves. Socioeconomic position is also used to
stratify results — but as a *determinant*, never as a component of
health (see [Boundaries](#boundaries)).

## Proxies are not the state of health

This is the project's most important measurement discipline. The state of
health is a **construct**: real, but not directly observable. Every
number we publish is a **proxy** — a measurement chosen because it tracks
the construct, built by someone else, for some other purpose, with its
own error.

Confusing a proxy for the construct is the central failure mode this
project guards against. Consequences of the distinction:

- **No proxy defines its domain.** Life expectancy does not *define*
  mortality's contribution to health; it proxies it. Self-rated health
  does not *define* wellbeing.
- **Proxies carry two kinds of error.** Ordinary measurement error, and
  construct error — the proxy may be reliable but track the wrong thing.
- **Proxies drift.** Administrative definitions, coding practices, and
  survey instruments change over time, so a series can move because the
  *proxy* changed, not the health ([nonstationarity](nonstationarity.qmd)).
- **Proxy disagreement is signal.** When two proxies for the same
  construct disagree, the right response is to investigate why, not to
  average the disagreement away.
- **Indices are models.** Any composite "health index" is a model built
  on chosen proxies and weights — a claim to be defended, not a
  measurement to be read off.
- **Causal analyses inherit all of this.** In milestones M4–M5 the
  proxies are variables, and their proxy status is part of the
  assumptions register.

Every indicator page must therefore state the construct it proxies, the
gap between proxy and construct, and the known limitations.

## Boundaries

The definition deliberately excludes:

- **Determinants of health** — income, education, housing, environment,
  service access. These enter analyses as explanatory variables and as
  stratification dimensions, never as components of health itself.
- **Health-system activity** — wait times, procedures, spending,
  staffing. These are inputs and system performance, not the population's
  state of health (they may *explain* it, which is a different role).
- **The absence of disease as sufficient.** The absence of disease is not
  full health [@who1948].
- **Any equivalence between self-reported and objective measures.**
  Both are proxies; neither is the truth.

## Resolution and fusion

The project uses **all available levels of resolution**, from individual
to provincial and beyond:

- individual (where microdata access and governance allow — see
  [Why BC only?](why-bc.qmd) and the roadmap's governance principles);
- neighbourhood and local health area (LHA);
- health service delivery area (HSDA) and health authority;
- provincial;
- external / non-BC (external drivers).

Different resolutions answer different questions and expose different
things: fine resolutions show local heterogeneity that coarse summaries
hide (and comparing coarse summaries to fine ones invites the ecological
fallacy). The project therefore:

1. records the **resolution** of every datum and every result;
2. **harmonises** across resolutions where definitions are compatible;
3. **fuses** pictures where that is useful, using multilevel/hierarchical
   models and other combination methods [@gelman2007];
4. treats any fused picture as a **model output** — reported with its
   assumptions and uncertainty, never as a fact.

## Temporal semantics

- Coverage targets **as far back as sources allow**, with each series
  carrying its observation window and definitional breaks handled
  explicitly.
- Health is represented as levels, slopes, and discontinuities — a
  trajectory, as set out in [Health is not stationary](nonstationarity.qmd).
- The definition itself is versioned; the thing defined drifts, and so
  does the definition.

## Boundaries of the definition itself

This document defines the *state of health*. It deliberately does not yet
settle: the exact indicator set (grows with the data landscape, M2), the
weights of any future index (a modelling choice, M3+), or the causal
claims that explain the state of health (M4–M5). Being honest about what
a definition does not cover is part of the definition.

## Revision process

The definition is revised when:

- the data landscape (M2) shows a domain is unmeasurable as conceived, or
  a measurable domain is missing;
- a proxy is shown to track its construct poorly;
- new evidence establishes a domain, or collapses a distinction;
- the population or measurement context shifts enough to invalidate part
  of the definition.

Each revision: increments the version, records the trigger and the
change, updates the [measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd)
and [glossary](../reference/glossary.qmd) as needed, and is reviewed by at
least one domain reviewer (roadmap M1 acceptance criterion).
